goals: Draw Lewis structures of simple covalent molecules and count sigma and pi bonds
Use bond parameters, bond polarity and dipole moment to compare molecules, and compare covalent with ionic compounds
Explain variable covalency, calculate formal charge and recognise incomplete and expanded octets

slides.narration: Welcome. In Part One we look at atoms that do not give electrons away but share them. We draw electron dot structures of methane, ammonia, water and carbon dioxide, then use bond lengths, energies and dipole moments to compare molecules, and finish with formal charge and the exceptions to the octet rule.

slides.heading: The covalent bond: single, double and triple
slides.body_md: A **covalent bond** forms when two atoms **share one or more electron pairs**, so that each attains a noble gas arrangement. It needs atoms that **each need electrons** and are close in electronegativity. One shared pair is a **single** bond, two a **double** bond and three a **triple** bond.

slides.narration: A covalent bond is formed by sharing electron pairs. It happens between atoms that both need electrons, for example two nonmetals. In hydrogen one pair is shared, giving a single bond. In oxygen two pairs are shared, a double bond, and in nitrogen three pairs are shared, a triple bond.

slides.body_md: In **ethane** the carbons share **1 pair**, in **ethene 2 pairs** and in **ethyne 3 pairs**. The total numbers of shared pairs are **7, 6 and 5**, and every carbon has an octet.

slides.heading: Sigma and pi bonds
slides.body_md: A **sigma (σ) bond** forms by **head-on overlap** of orbitals along the bond axis; it is the first bond between two atoms. A **pi (π) bond** forms by **sideways overlap** of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis, and is **weaker**. Single bond: 1 σ; double: 1 σ + 1 π; triple: 1 σ + 2 π.

slides.narration: A sigma bond is formed by head on overlap along the line joining the nuclei, and it is the strongest kind of overlap. A pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis. A single bond is one sigma bond, a double bond is one sigma and one pi, and a triple bond is one sigma and two pi bonds.

slides.heading: Worked example: bonds in acrylonitrile
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Count the σ and π bonds in acrylonitrile, $\ce{CH2=CH-C#N}$.

Bonds: 3 C–H (3 σ); C–C single (1 σ); C=C double (1 σ + 1 π); C≡N triple (1 σ + 2 π).

σ bonds $= 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6$; π bonds $= 1 + 2 = 3$. Check: 9 bonds counted as lines (3 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 9) $= 6 + 3$.

visual.alt: Table counting the sigma and pi bonds in acrylonitrile

Each contributes one sigma bond, so there are six sigma bonds. The double bond adds one pi bond and the triple bond adds two, giving three pi bonds.

slides.heading: Bond parameters: length, enthalpy and order
slides.body_md: **Bond length** is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei. **Bond enthalpy** is the energy to break one mole of the bond in the gas phase. **Bond order** is the number of shared pairs. A higher bond order gives a **shorter and stronger** bond. **Bond angle** is the angle between two bonds at one atom.

visual.alt: Table of bond order, length and enthalpy for selected bonds

slides.narration: Bond length is the distance between the two nuclei, and bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of the bond. As the bond order increases from one to three, the bond gets shorter and stronger. Carbon carbon bonds show this clearly, with the triple bond only one hundred twenty picometres long but very strong.

slides.body_md: As two hydrogen atoms approach, **attraction** lowers the energy until, at **74 pm**, **repulsion** between the nuclei and electrons balances it. The depth of the well, **436 kJ mol⁻¹**, is the bond enthalpy.

slides.heading: Polar bonds and dipole moment
slides.body_md: When two atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom: a **polar covalent bond**, with partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻. The **dipole moment** is $\mu = q \times d$, in **debye** (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m). It is a **vector**, so a molecule with polar bonds may still have μ = 0.

visual.alt: Table of dipole moment, bond length and the dipole moment for a fully ionic bond for the hydrogen halides

slides.narration: When two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared pair is drawn towards one of them, and the bond is polar. The dipole moment is the charge times the distance, measured in debye. It is a vector, which means that the direction matters, and a molecule with polar bonds can still have no overall dipole moment.

slides.heading: Shape decides whether the molecule is polar
slides.body_md: In **CO₂** the two C=O dipoles point opposite ways and cancel (μ = 0). In **BF₃** three dipoles at 120° cancel. In **H₂O** the dipoles at 104.5° add to **1.85 D**: polar.

slides.heading: Worked example: percentage ionic character of HCl
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** HCl has $\mu = 1.03$ D and bond length 127.4 pm. Find the percentage ionic character. ($e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C; 1 D $= 3.336 \times 10^{-30}$ C m)

If completely ionic: $\mu = e \times d = 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \times 127.4 \times 10^{-12} = 20.409 \times 10^{-30}$ C m $= 6.12$ D.

Ionic character $= \dfrac{1.03}{6.12} \times 100 = 16.8\ \%$.

rows: μ if H⁺ Cl⁻ were fully ionic

visual.alt: Table of the dipole-moment calculation for HCl

slides.narration: First find the dipole moment the molecule would have if it were completely ionic. Multiply the electron charge by the bond length, and convert to debye. For hydrogen chloride this is about six point one debye. The measured value is only one point zero three, so the bond is about seventeen percent ionic and the rest covalent.

slides.heading: Quick check: the most polar bond
slides.body_md: The larger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the electronegativity values given in the question. Subtract the value for hydrogen from the value for the other atom in each bond, then pick the bond with the largest difference, since a larger difference pulls the shared pair further towards one atom.

slides.heading: Covalent compared with ionic compounds
slides.body_md: Covalent compounds consist of **molecules** held together by **weak forces**, so they are usually gases, liquids or low-melting solids, **non-conductors**, soluble in non-polar solvents. Ionic compounds are **lattices of ions**, so they are hard, brittle, high-melting, and conduct when molten or dissolved.

visual.alt: Table comparing covalent and ionic compounds

slides.narration: Covalent compounds are made of molecules, and the forces between molecules are weak, so they melt and boil easily and do not conduct electricity. Ionic compounds are lattices of ions held by strong electrostatic forces, so they have high melting points, and conduct when molten or dissolved. Their reactions in solution are fast.

slides.heading: Variable covalency: P, S and Cl
slides.body_md: **Covalency** is the number of bonds an atom forms. Atoms of the third period have vacant **3d orbitals**, so electrons can be **promoted** to give more unpaired electrons: P shows **3 and 5**, S shows **2, 4 and 6**, Cl shows **1, 3, 5 and 7**. Second-period atoms (N, O, F) cannot.

visual.alt: Table of ground and excited state configurations and covalencies of P, S and Cl

slides.narration: Covalency is the number of bonds an atom forms. Atoms of the third period have empty d orbitals, so one electron can be promoted to give more unpaired electrons. Phosphorus shows covalencies of three and five, sulfur shows two, four and six, and chlorine shows one, three, five and seven. Nitrogen cannot, as it has no d orbitals.

slides.heading: Formal charge
slides.body_md: **Formal charge = V − L − B/2**, where V is the number of valence electrons of the free atom, L the non-bonding electrons and B the bonding electrons. The formal charges add up to the charge on the species, and the best Lewis structure has charges as small as possible, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

visual.alt: Table of formal charge calculations for NH4 plus, H3O plus, CO and O3

slides.narration: Formal charge is the number of valence electrons of the free atom, minus the nonbonding electrons, minus half of the bonding electrons. The formal charges in a structure must add up to the overall charge of the species. The best structure has the smallest formal charges, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

slides.heading: Deviations from the octet rule
slides.body_md: **Incomplete octets:** BeCl₂ (4 electrons round Be), BF₃ (6 round B). **Expanded octets:** PCl₅ (10 round P), SF₆ (12 round S); these use vacant 3d orbitals and are possible only from the third period on.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Covalent bond: shared electron pairs; single, double, triple bonds = 1, 2, 3 pairs = 1 σ; 1 σ + 1 π; 1 σ + 2 π.
Higher bond order: shorter and stronger bond (C–C 154 pm, 347; C≡C 120 pm, 837 kJ mol⁻¹).
Dipole moment μ = q × d (debye); a symmetrical shape can cancel polar bonds (CO₂, BF₃).
Covalent compounds: low melting points, non-conductors; ionic: high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved.
Variable covalency from 3d promotion (P: 3, 5; S: 2, 4, 6; Cl: 1, 3, 5, 7); formal charge = V − L − B/2; incomplete (BF₃) and expanded (PCl₅, SF₆) octets.

rows: σ head-on and stronger; π sideways
μ is the vector sum of bond dipoles

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Covalent bonds are shared electron pairs, and they can be single, double or triple, made of sigma and pi bonds. A higher bond order means a shorter and stronger bond. The dipole moment is a vector, so shape decides whether a molecule is polar. Third period atoms can have variable covalency and expanded octets, and formal charge helps to choose the best structure.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Count σ bonds as the number of lines (bonds) and π bonds as the extra lines of double and triple bonds.
Say "the dipoles cancel because the molecule is linear (or symmetrical)", not "the bonds are non-polar".
Convert bond length to metres and the dipole moment from C m to debye; give the percentage with its unit.
Formal charge: halve the bonding electrons, and check that the charges add up to the charge on the species.
Give the electron count (4, 6, 10 or 12) when naming an octet deviation.

The bond is polar; the dipoles cancel by symmetry

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. We begin with Fajan rules, which explain why a bond between a metal and a nonmetal can have covalent character. Then we use electron pair repulsion to predict molecular shapes, and finish with hybridisation, which links the orbitals used to the geometry we observe.

slides.heading: Fajan’s rules
slides.body_md: An ionic bond has **covalent character** when the cation **polarises** (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion. This is greater when **(1)** the cation is **small** with a **high charge**, **(2)** the anion is **large** with a **high charge**, and **(3)** the cation has a **non-noble-gas** outer shell (such as Ag⁺).

visual.alt: Table of Fajan rules with examples

slides.narration: Fajan rules say that an ionic bond becomes more covalent when the cation polarises the anion strongly. This happens when the cation is small and highly charged, and when the anion is large and highly charged. A cation without a noble gas outer shell, such as silver, also polarises strongly.

slides.heading: Worked example: ordering chlorides by covalent character
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange NaCl, MgCl₂ and AlCl₃ in order of increasing covalent character using the charge-to-radius ratio $z/r$ of the cation (Na⁺ 102 pm, Mg²⁺ 72 pm, Al³⁺ 53.5 pm).

$z/r$ for Na⁺ $= 1/102 = 9.8 \times 10^{-3}$; Mg²⁺ $= 2/72 = 27.8 \times 10^{-3}$; Al³⁺ $= 3/53.5 = 56.1 \times 10^{-3}$ pm⁻¹.

Order: **NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃**.

visual.alt: Table of charge to radius ratio and character for NaCl, MgCl2 and AlCl3

slides.narration: Divide the charge of each cation by its radius. Sodium gives about ten, magnesium about twenty eight, and aluminium about fifty six, in units of ten to the minus three per picometre. The larger the ratio, the more the cation polarises the chloride ion, so the order is sodium chloride, then magnesium chloride, then aluminium chloride.

slides.heading: Quick check: LiCl and its relatives
slides.body_md: Equal charges, so compare the cation sizes.
slides.narration: Quick check. All four cations carry the same single charge, and the anion is the same, so only the size of the cation matters. Decide whether the smallest or the largest cation is the better at distorting the chloride ion.

slides.heading: VSEPR theory: electron pairs repel
slides.body_md: In the **valence shell electron pair repulsion** theory the electron pairs round a central atom (**bond pairs** and **lone pairs**) arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Repulsion order: **lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair**. A multiple bond counts as **one** domain.

nodes.label: Count the valence electrons round the central atom
Find the number of bond pairs and lone pairs
Arrange the pairs as far apart as possible
Name the shape from the positions of the atoms only
Adjust the angles: lone pairs compress them

visual.alt: Flow chart of the steps for predicting molecular shape by VSEPR theory

slides.narration: In the electron pair repulsion theory the pairs of electrons around the central atom spread out as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, so the order of repulsion is lone pair with lone pair, then lone pair with bond pair, then bond pair with bond pair. A double or triple bond counts as a single region of electrons.

slides.body_md: **2 pairs:** linear, 180°. **3:** trigonal planar, 120°. **4:** tetrahedral, 109.5°. **5:** trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°. **6:** octahedral, 90°. Examples: BeCl₂, BF₃, CH₄, PCl₅, SF₆.

slides.narration: With only bond pairs, the shapes are simple. Two pairs give a linear molecule. Three pairs give a trigonal planar molecule. Four pairs give a tetrahedron. Five pairs give a trigonal bipyramid, with two kinds of position. Six pairs give an octahedron. Beryllium chloride, boron trifluoride, methane, phosphorus pentachloride and sulfur hexafluoride are examples.

slides.heading: Lone pairs change the shape
slides.body_md: The **electron-pair geometry** is set by all the pairs; the **shape** is named from the atoms only. **Lone pairs** take more room, so they **compress** bond angles and, in the trigonal bipyramid, sit in the **equatorial** positions.

visual.alt: Table of electron-pair geometry, shape, example and bond angle for molecules with lone pairs

slides.narration: The geometry of all the electron pairs decides the arrangement, but the name of the shape comes from the atoms alone. Lone pairs take up more room, so they squeeze the bond angles. In a trigonal bipyramid they sit in the equatorial positions, where there is more space. Ammonia is pyramidal, water is bent, and sulfur tetrafluoride is see saw shaped.

slides.narration: Here are five more shapes. Start from a trigonal bipyramid and put lone pairs in the equatorial positions: one lone pair gives a see saw, two give a T shape, and three give a linear molecule. Start from an octahedron: one lone pair gives a square pyramid, and two lone pairs opposite each other give a square planar molecule.

slides.heading: Worked example: shapes of SF₄ and XeF₂
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Predict the shapes of $\ce{SF4}$ and $\ce{XeF2}$.

**SF₄:** S has 6 valence electrons; 4 F add 4 → 10 electrons = **5 pairs**: 4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair. Trigonal bipyramidal pairs, lone pair equatorial → **see-saw**.

**XeF₂:** Xe has 8; 2 F add 2 → 10 = **5 pairs**: 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs. Lone pairs equatorial → F atoms axial → **linear, 180°**.

visual.alt: Table of the VSEPR analysis of SF4 and XeF2

slides.narration: For sulfur tetrafluoride, sulfur has six valence electrons and the four fluorine atoms add four more, making ten electrons or five pairs. Four are bond pairs and one is a lone pair, so the shape is see saw. For xenon difluoride, xenon has eight electrons and two more are added, again five pairs, with two bond pairs and three lone pairs, so the molecule is linear.

slides.heading: Hybridisation: why equal bonds from unequal orbitals
slides.body_md: Carbon has 2s² 2p² but forms **four equal bonds** in methane. In **hybridisation** atomic orbitals of the same atom with slightly different energies **mix** to form the **same number of equivalent hybrid orbitals**, directed in space to give the molecule its shape. An electron is first **promoted** if needed.

nodes.label: Promote an electron to a vacant orbital of nearby energy
Mix the s, p (and d) orbitals
Form equivalent hybrid orbitals, one electron each
Each overlaps head-on with another atom: a σ bond

visual.alt: Flow chart of promotion, mixing, hybrid orbitals and sigma bond formation

slides.narration: Carbon has two paired s electrons and two unpaired p electrons, yet it forms four equal bonds in methane. Hybridisation explains this. An electron is promoted, then the s and p orbitals mix to give the same number of equivalent hybrid orbitals, each holding one electron. Each hybrid orbital then overlaps head on with an orbital of another atom to form a sigma bond.

slides.heading: Promotion and hybridisation of Be, B, C, P and S
slides.body_md: Be: **sp** (2 orbitals). B: **sp²** (3). C: **sp³** (4). P: **sp³d** (5, with a 3d orbital). S: **sp³d²** (6, with two 3d orbitals). The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of orbitals mixed.

slides.narration: The hybrid orbitals point in definite directions. Two s p hybrids are in a straight line. Three s p two hybrids lie in a plane at one hundred twenty degrees. slides.heading: Hybridisation and shape together
slides.body_md: Count the **electron pairs** round the central atom (bond pairs + lone pairs; a multiple bond counts once): **2 → sp**, **3 → sp²**, **4 → sp³**, **5 → sp³d**, **6 → sp³d²**. The shape then follows from the number of lone pairs.

visual.alt: Table linking the number of electron pairs, hybridisation, geometry and examples

slides.narration: Here is the shortcut. Count the electron pairs round the central atom, counting a double or triple bond once. Two pairs mean s p. Three mean s p two. Four mean s p three. Five mean s p three d, and six mean s p three d two. The shape then depends on how many of those pairs are lone pairs.

slides.heading: Worked example: hybridisation by counting pairs
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the hybridisation of the central atom in $\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{PCl5}$ and ethene.

**NH₃:** 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 4 → **sp³**. **H₂O:** 2 + 2 = 4 → **sp³**. **PCl₅:** 5 bond pairs = 5 → **sp³d**. **Ethene:** each C has 3 σ bonds, the π bond adds no domain → 3 → **sp²**.

headers: Pairs (or σ bonds) round the central atom

visual.alt: Table of hybridisation of NH3, H2O, PCl5 and ethene by counting electron pairs

slides.narration: Count the regions of electrons round each central atom. In ammonia there are three bond pairs and one lone pair, four in all, so the atom is s p three hybridised. Water also has four, so it is s p three. Phosphorus pentachloride has five, so s p three d. In ethene each carbon has three sigma bonds, and the pi bond adds no new region, so it is s p two.

slides.heading: Hybridisation in ethane, ethene and ethyne
slides.body_md: **Ethane:** each C is **sp³** (4 σ). **Ethene:** each C is **sp²** (3 σ + 1 π; the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways). **Ethyne:** each C is **sp** (2 σ + 2 π; two unhybridised p orbitals). More s character gives a **shorter, stronger** bond.

visual.alt: Table of the hybridisation of carbon, bond type and length in ethane, ethene and ethyne

slides.narration: In ethane each carbon is s p three hybridised, with four sigma bonds. In ethene each carbon is s p two, and the leftover p orbitals overlap sideways to form a pi bond. In ethyne each carbon is s p, with two leftover p orbitals that form two pi bonds. The carbon carbon bond becomes shorter as the s character increases.

slides.heading: Quick check: hybridisation in ethene
slides.body_md: Count the sigma bonds round one carbon; the pi bond uses an unhybridised p orbital.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count how many sigma bonds each carbon forms. The pi bond is made from an unhybridised p orbital and does not need a hybrid orbital, so use the number of sigma bonds to choose the hybridisation.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Fajan: covalent character rises with a small, highly charged cation and a large, highly charged anion (LiCl > NaCl; AlCl₃ > MgCl₂ > NaCl).
VSEPR: pairs repel; lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair; shapes NH₃ pyramidal, H₂O bent, SF₄ see-saw, XeF₂ linear.
Hybridisation: pairs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 → sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d².
Ethane sp³, ethene sp², ethyne sp; σ bonds from hybrid orbitals, π bonds from unhybridised p orbitals.

visual.alt: Summary table of pairs, hybridisation and shape

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part Two. Fajan rules say that a small, highly charged cation and a large anion give more covalent character. VSEPR theory predicts shapes from the repulsion of electron pairs, with lone pairs compressing the angles. Hybridisation links the number of electron pairs to the type of orbitals used, from s p for two pairs to s p three d two for six pairs.

notes.title: Covalent Bonding, VSEPR and Hybridisation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The covalent bond, Lewis structures, sigma and pi bonds
sections.body_md:
A **covalent bond** is formed by the **sharing of electron pairs** between two atoms so that each reaches a noble gas arrangement (octet; duplet for H). It forms between atoms that each need electrons and have similar, high electronegativity. One shared pair gives a **single** bond, two a **double** bond and three a **triple** bond.

**Lewis structures:** $\ce{CH4}$ (4 shared pairs), $\ce{NH3}$ (3 shared pairs, 1 lone pair on N), $\ce{H2O}$ (2 shared pairs, 2 lone pairs on O), $\ce{CO2}$ (O=C=O, 4 shared pairs, 2 lone pairs on each O), ethane (7 shared pairs), ethene (6; C=C has 2) and ethyne (5; C≡C has 3).

A **sigma (σ) bond** is formed by **head-on** overlap along the bond axis; a **pi (π) bond** by **sideways** overlap of parallel p orbitals, and is weaker. Single = 1 σ; double = 1 σ + 1 π; triple = 1 σ + 2 π. So H₂ has 1 σ; O₂ has 1 σ + 1 π; N₂ has 1 σ + 2 π.

key_terms.definition_md: A bond formed by the sharing of one or more electron pairs between two atoms.
A bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the line joining the nuclei.
A bond formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the bond axis.
A pair of valence electrons on one atom that is not used in bonding.

sections.heading: 2. Bond parameters, polarity and dipole moment; covalent against ionic compounds
sections.body_md:
**Bond length** is the distance between the nuclei; **bond enthalpy** is the energy to break one mole of the bond (gas phase); **bond order** is the number of shared pairs; **bond angle** is the angle between two bonds. Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond: C–C 154 pm, 347 kJ mol⁻¹; C=C 134 pm, 611; C≡C 120 pm, 837.

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is **polar**. **Dipole moment** $\mu = q \times d$ (debye; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m); it is a **vector**: CO₂ (linear) and BF₃ (planar) have μ = 0 although their bonds are polar; H₂O (bent) has μ ≈ 1.85 D. Percentage ionic character $= \mu_\text{observed}/\mu_\text{ionic} \times 100$, with $\mu_\text{ionic} = e \times d$: HCl 16.8 %, HF 43.4 %.

**Covalent compounds:** molecules, weak forces, low melting and boiling points, non-conductors, soluble in non-polar solvents. **Ionic compounds:** lattices of ions, high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved, soluble in water.

key_terms.definition_md: The energy required to break one mole of a bond in the gaseous state.
The product of the charge and the distance between the charges, μ = q × d, measured in debye.
A covalent bond in which the shared pair is displaced towards the more electronegative atom.

sections.heading: 3. Variable covalency, formal charge and deviations from the octet rule
sections.body_md:
**Covalency** is the number of covalent bonds an atom forms. Atoms of the third period and below promote an electron to a vacant **d orbital** to increase the number of unpaired electrons: **P: 3, 5** (3s² 3p³ → 3s¹ 3p³ 3d¹); **S: 2, 4, 6**; **Cl: 1, 3, 5, 7**. Second-period atoms have no d orbitals (N forms NCl₃, not NCl₅).

**Formal charge** = V − L − B/2. Examples: N in NH₄⁺ = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1; O in H₃O⁺ = +1; in CO the carbon is −1 and the oxygen +1. The best structure has the smallest formal charges and the sum equal to the charge on the species.

**Incomplete octets:** BeCl₂ (4 electrons on Be), BF₃ (6 on B). **Expanded octets:** PCl₅ (10 on P), SF₆ (12 on S), using vacant 3d orbitals.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of covalent bonds formed by an atom.
The charge an atom would have if the bonding electrons were shared equally: V − L − B/2.
A central atom of the third period or below with more than eight electrons round it.

sections.heading: 4. Fajan’s rules
sections.body_md:
An ionic bond has some **covalent character** when the cation **polarises** the anion. It increases with **(1) a small cation, (2) a high charge on the cation, (3) a large anion, (4) a high charge on the anion**, and with a cation of non-noble-gas type (e.g. Ag⁺, with 18 outer electrons). The **ionic potential** $z/r$ measures the polarising power: Li⁺ 13.2, Na⁺ 9.8, Mg²⁺ 27.8, Al³⁺ 56.1 (× 10⁻³ pm⁻¹).

Hence LiCl is more covalent than NaCl (and is soluble in ethanol); AlCl₃ > MgCl₂ > NaCl (AlCl₃ sublimes easily); LiI is more covalent than LiF.

key_terms.definition_md: The distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a neighbouring cation.
The ability of a cation to distort an anion; it rises with charge and falls with size.

sections.heading: 5. VSEPR theory and shapes of molecules
sections.body_md:
Electron pairs (bond pairs and lone pairs) round the central atom repel each other and take positions as far apart as possible. **Repulsion order:** lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. A multiple bond counts as one region.

Number of pairs and lone pairs from the valence electrons: pairs = (electrons of the central atom + one for each single-bonded monovalent atom ∓ charge) / 2.

**2 pairs:** linear (BeCl₂, 180°). **3:** trigonal planar (BF₃, 120°); with 1 lone pair, bent (SO₂). **4:** tetrahedral (CH₄, 109.5°); 1 lone pair, pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); 2 lone pairs, bent (H₂O, 104.5°). **5:** trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅); 1 lone pair, see-saw (SF₄); 2, T-shaped (ClF₃); 3, linear (XeF₂); the lone pairs are equatorial. **6:** octahedral (SF₆); 1 lone pair, square pyramidal (BrF₅); 2, square planar (XeF₄).

key_terms.definition_md: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory: the shape of a molecule is decided by the repulsion between the electron pairs round the central atom.
A position in the plane of the trigonal bipyramid, at 120° to the others; lone pairs prefer it.

sections.heading: 6. Hybridisation involving s, p and d orbitals
sections.body_md:
**Hybridisation** is the mixing of atomic orbitals of the same atom, of nearly equal energy, to give the **same number of equivalent hybrid orbitals** directed in space at fixed angles. After promotion, each hybrid orbital holds one electron (or a lone pair) and forms a σ bond by head-on overlap.

**sp** (BeCl₂, linear, 180°); **sp²** (BF₃, planar, 120°); **sp³** (CH₄, 109.5°; NH₃ and H₂O have lone pairs in sp³ orbitals); **sp³d** (PCl₅, trigonal bipyramidal); **sp³d²** (SF₆, octahedral, 90°). The hybridisation follows from the **number of electron pairs** (a multiple bond counts once).

**Carbon compounds:** ethane, sp³ (C–C single, 1 σ); ethene, sp² (C=C: 1 σ + 1 π from unhybridised p orbitals); ethyne, sp (C≡C: 1 σ + 2 π). The shorter bond has more s character.

key_terms.definition_md: The mixing of atomic orbitals of one atom to form equivalent orbitals of the same number, with fixed directions in space.
One of the equivalent orbitals formed by hybridisation.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Counting a triple bond as three sigma bonds, or a double bond as two sigma bonds.
- Writing "CO₂ is non-polar because the bonds are non-polar": the bonds are polar and the dipoles cancel by symmetry.
- Using the whole bonding electron count in formal charge (halve it), or forgetting to check the sum.
- Saying nitrogen can form NF₅ or have an expanded octet.
- Naming the shape of NH₃ "tetrahedral", or forgetting that lone pairs sit in equatorial positions in a trigonal bipyramid.
- Mixing up the hybridisation (from all the pairs) with the shape (from the atoms only).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Lewis structure: shared pairs (1), lone pairs and octets (1).
- Dipole-moment numericals: μ_ionic = e × d (1), conversion to debye (1), percentage (1).
- VSEPR: electron count (1), numbers of bond pairs and lone pairs (1), shape and angle (1).
- Hybridisation: orbitals mixed (1), geometry (1), σ and π bonds where asked (1).

cards.front_md: What is a covalent bond?
cards.back_md: A bond formed by the sharing of one or more electron pairs between two atoms.

cards.front_md: How many pairs are shared in single, double and triple bonds?
cards.back_md: One, two and three pairs.

cards.front_md: Lewis structure of water: shared pairs and lone pairs?
cards.back_md: Two shared pairs; two lone pairs on oxygen.

cards.front_md: Lewis structure of CO₂?
cards.back_md: O=C=O: four shared pairs and two lone pairs on each oxygen.

cards.front_md: Shared pairs in ethane, ethene, ethyne?
cards.back_md: 7, 6 and 5 (between the carbons: 1, 2 and 3).

cards.front_md: What is a sigma bond?
cards.back_md: A bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the line joining the nuclei.

cards.front_md: What is a pi bond?
cards.back_md: A bond formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis; weaker than σ.

cards.front_md: Sigma and pi bonds in N₂?
cards.back_md: One σ and two π.

cards.front_md: Sigma and pi bonds in ethene?
cards.back_md: 5 σ (4 C–H, 1 C–C) and 1 π.

cards.front_md: Define bond enthalpy.
cards.back_md: The energy needed to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase.

cards.front_md: How do bond length and enthalpy change with bond order?
cards.back_md: Length decreases and enthalpy increases.

cards.front_md: C–C, C=C, C≡C: bond lengths?
What is a polar covalent bond?
cards.back_md: One in which the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, giving partial charges.

cards.front_md: Dipole moment: formula and unit?
cards.back_md: $\mu = q \times d$, in debye; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m.

cards.front_md: Why is CO₂ non-polar?
cards.back_md: It is linear, so the two equal C=O dipoles cancel.

cards.front_md: Percentage ionic character?
cards.back_md: $\mu_\text{observed} / (e \times d) \times 100$.

cards.front_md: Two differences: covalent against ionic compounds?
cards.back_md: Covalent: low melting points, non-conductors; ionic: high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved.

cards.front_md: What is covalency?
cards.back_md: The number of covalent bonds formed by an atom.

cards.front_md: Covalencies of P, S and Cl?
Why can P but not N have covalency 5?
cards.back_md: P has vacant 3d orbitals for promotion; N has no 2d orbitals.

cards.front_md: Formal charge formula?
cards.back_md: $V - L - \tfrac12 B$.

cards.front_md: Formal charge on N in NH₄⁺?
Examples of incomplete octets?
cards.back_md: BeCl₂ (4 electrons on Be) and BF₃ (6 on B).

cards.front_md: Examples of expanded octets?
cards.back_md: PCl₅ (10 on P) and SF₆ (12 on S).

cards.front_md: State Fajan’s rules in brief.
cards.back_md: More covalent character with a small, highly charged cation and a large, highly charged anion; non-noble-gas cations polarise more.

cards.front_md: Which is more covalent, LiCl or NaCl? Why?
cards.back_md: LiCl: Li⁺ is smaller, so it has greater charge density and polarises Cl⁻ more.

cards.front_md: Order of covalent character: NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃?
cards.back_md: NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃ (z/r rises).

cards.front_md: State the VSEPR repulsion order.
cards.back_md: Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

cards.front_md: Shapes and angles of NH₃, H₂O and CH₄?
cards.back_md: Pyramidal 107°; bent 104.5°; tetrahedral 109.5°.

cards.front_md: Shapes of SF₄, ClF₃, XeF₂?
cards.back_md: See-saw; T-shaped; linear (lone pairs equatorial).

cards.front_md: Hybridisation and shape: BeCl₂, BF₃, CH₄, PCl₅, SF₆?
cards.back_md: sp linear; sp² trigonal planar; sp³ tetrahedral; sp³d trigonal bipyramidal; sp³d² octahedral.

cards.front_md: Hybridisation of carbon in ethane, ethene and ethyne?
cards.back_md: sp³, sp² and sp.

questions.stem_md: A chemist wants to predict which pair of elements will join by sharing electrons rather than by transferring them. The best choice is:

options.text_md: nitrogen and hydrogen, two non-metals that each need electrons to complete their outer shells
sodium and fluorine, a metal with low ionisation enthalpy and a non-metal
potassium and chlorine, which differ greatly in electronegativity
neon and argon, whose outer shells are already full

questions.solution_md: A covalent bond forms between atoms that both need electrons and are close in electronegativity, such as N and H. The metal–non-metal pairs transfer electrons, and the noble gases form no bonds — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A fire-extinguisher cylinder is filled with carbon dioxide. In the Lewis structure of the molecule, the numbers of shared pairs and of lone pairs are respectively:

options.text_md: 4 shared pairs and 4 lone pairs
2 shared pairs and 6 lone pairs
4 shared pairs and 2 lone pairs
3 shared pairs and 5 lone pairs

questions.solution_md: O=C=O: each C=O is a double bond (2 shared pairs), giving 4 shared pairs; each oxygen keeps 2 lone pairs, giving 4 lone pairs. Total electrons: 2 × 4 + 2 × 4 = 16 = 4 + 6 + 6 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A polymer chemist studies propene, CH₃–CH=CH₂, the monomer of polypropylene. The numbers of sigma and pi bonds in one molecule are respectively:

options.text_md: 8 sigma and 1 pi
7 sigma and 2 pi
9 sigma and 0 pi
6 sigma and 3 pi

questions.solution_md: Single bonds are σ: 6 C–H and 1 C–C = 7; the C=C double bond has 1 σ and 1 π. Total 8 σ and 1 π — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Nitrogen gas is used to keep food fresh in sealed packets. The bonding in its molecule is best described as:

options.text_md: one sigma bond and two pi bonds between the atoms, a bond order of 3
three sigma bonds between the atoms, a bond order of 3
one sigma bond and one pi bond between the atoms, a bond order of 2
two sigma bonds and one pi bond between the atoms, a bond order of 3

questions.solution_md: Two N atoms (5 valence electrons each) share three pairs; the first pair overlaps head-on (σ) and the other two sideways (two π bonds at right angles) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Ethene, C₂H₄, is the gas that ripens fruit in storage rooms. The number of electron pairs shared in one molecule is:
questions.solution_md: Valence electrons: 2 × 4 + 4 × 1 = 12, all shared in the structure H₂C=CH₂: 4 C–H pairs + 2 pairs in C=C = 6 shared pairs — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A pi bond is formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the line joining the two nuclei.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Head-on overlap along the internuclear axis gives a sigma bond; a pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis.

questions.stem_md: The bond order of the nitrogen molecule, N≡N, is ___.
questions.solution_md: Three shared pairs join the nitrogen atoms, so the bond order is 3.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The H–H bond in a hydrogen molecule is a single covalent bond.

**Reason (R):** The two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons, and each atom then has the duplet of helium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. One shared pair makes the bond single and gives each H two electrons, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each molecule with the numbers of sigma and pi bonds that it contains.

options.text_md: H₂
O₂
N₂
C₂H₂

match_right.text_md: one σ bond and one π bond
three σ bonds and two π bonds
one σ bond and two π bonds

questions.solution_md: H₂ → r (one σ); O₂ → p (one σ and one π); N₂ → s (one σ and two π); C₂H₂ → q (three σ and two π).

questions.stem_md: Explain how a sigma bond differs from a pi bond in the kind of orbital overlap and in strength, taking the nitrogen molecule as your example.

answer.model_answer_md: A sigma bond is formed by head-on (end-to-end) overlap of orbitals along the line joining the nuclei, and it is stronger because the overlap is greater. A pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis, so the overlap is smaller and the bond weaker. In N₂ (N≡N) one of the three bonds is a σ bond and the other two are π bonds at right angles.

questions.solution_md: σ: head-on and stronger; π: sideways and weaker; N₂ has 1 σ and 2 π.

marking_scheme.step: π: sideways overlap, weaker; N₂ has 1 σ and 2 π

questions.stem_md: Acrylonitrile, CH₂=CH–C≡N, is the starting material for acrylic fibres. Draw its structure showing every bond, and count the sigma and pi bonds in one molecule.

answer.model_answer_md: Structure: H₂C=CH–C≡N, with 2 C–H bonds on the first carbon, 1 C–H on the second, and a lone pair on nitrogen. σ bonds: 3 C–H + 1 C–C + 1 (in C=C) + 1 (in C≡N) = 6. π bonds: 1 (in C=C) + 2 (in C≡N) = 3. Check: single bonds give 1 σ each, a double bond 1 σ + 1 π, a triple bond 1 σ + 2 π.

questions.solution_md: 6 σ bonds and 3 π bonds.

marking_scheme.step: Correct structure with the double and the triple bond

questions.stem_md: Write the electron-dot structures of ethane, ethene and ethyne, stating for each how many electron pairs are shared between the two carbon atoms and the total number of shared pairs.

answer.model_answer_md: Ethane H₃C–CH₃: the carbons share 1 pair; total shared pairs 7 (6 C–H + 1 C–C). Ethene H₂C=CH₂: the carbons share 2 pairs; total 6 (4 C–H + 2). Ethyne HC≡CH: the carbons share 3 pairs; total 5 (2 C–H + 3). In each structure every carbon has 8 electrons and every hydrogen 2.

questions.solution_md: C–C pairs: 1, 2, 3; total shared pairs 7, 6, 5.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw the electron-dot structures of carbon dioxide and of ethyne, showing all shared pairs and lone pairs. [3]

(b) State the number of sigma bonds and pi bonds in each of the two molecules. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) CO₂: O::C::O, each oxygen with two lone pairs (two shared pairs between C and each O, 4 shared pairs and 4 lone pairs in all). C₂H₂: H:C:::C:H, three shared pairs between the carbons and one pair in each C–H bond, with no lone pairs.

(b) CO₂: two σ bonds and two π bonds (each C=O has 1 σ and 1 π). C₂H₂: three σ bonds (2 C–H and 1 C–C) and two π bonds (in C≡C).

questions.solution_md: Dot structures; CO₂ 2σ + 2π; C₂H₂ 3σ + 2π.

questions.stem_md: A student tabulates length and enthalpy for three carbon–carbon bonds: C–C 154 pm, 347 kJ mol⁻¹; C=C 134 pm, 611 kJ mol⁻¹; C≡C 120 pm, 837 kJ mol⁻¹. The correct conclusion is that, as the bond order rises:

options.text_md: the bond becomes longer and its bond enthalpy becomes larger
the bond becomes shorter and its bond enthalpy becomes smaller
the bond becomes shorter and its bond enthalpy becomes larger
the bond length and the bond enthalpy both stay nearly constant

questions.solution_md: From C–C to C≡C the length falls (154 → 120 pm) and the enthalpy rises (347 → 837 kJ mol⁻¹), because more shared pairs pull the nuclei closer and hold them more strongly — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Pauling electronegativities (given) are H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3, O 3.5 and F 4. Which of these bonds is the most polar?

options.text_md: H–C (difference 0.4)
H–N (difference 0.9)
H–O (difference 1.4)
H–F (difference 1.9)

questions.solution_md: The differences are 0.4, 0.9, 1.4, 1.9; the largest belongs to the H–F bond, so it is the most polar — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Each C=O bond in carbon dioxide is polar, yet the gas has a zero dipole moment. The reason is that:

options.text_md: carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity
the C=O bonds are non-polar covalent bonds
the lone pairs on oxygen cancel the polarity of the bonds
the molecule is linear, so the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel

questions.solution_md: O is more electronegative than C, so each C=O bond is polar; but in a linear molecule the two bond dipoles are equal and opposite and their resultant is zero — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student lists four gases from a laboratory cylinder store: NH₃, H₂O, BF₃ and SO₂. Which has a zero dipole moment?

options.text_md: NH₃, because its three N–H bonds are identical
BF₃, because its three polar B–F bonds lie symmetrically in a plane at 120°
H₂O, because it contains only one kind of bond
SO₂, because the two S=O bonds are identical

questions.solution_md: Only BF₃ is symmetrical (trigonal planar), so its three bond dipoles cancel. NH₃ is pyramidal, H₂O and SO₂ are bent, and all three have non-zero resultants — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A liquid boils at 77 °C, does not conduct electricity even when pure, mixes freely with benzene and does not dissolve in water. It is most likely:

options.text_md: an ionic compound with a lattice of ions
a covalent compound made of non-polar molecules
a metal in the liquid state
a polar covalent compound that ionises in water

questions.solution_md: Low boiling point, no conduction, solubility in a non-polar solvent and insolubility in water are all typical of non-polar covalent molecules — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Carbon tetrachloride dissolves readily in water because its four C–Cl bonds are polar.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The C–Cl bonds are polar, but the molecule is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel; the molecule is non-polar and does not dissolve in water.

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of dipole moment is the ___ metre (C m).
questions.solution_md: Dipole moment = charge × distance, so its SI unit is the coulomb metre (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m).

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen bromide has a measured dipole moment of 0.79 D and a bond length of 141.4 pm. Taking e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m, calculate the percentage ionic character of the H–Br bond.
questions.solution_md: For a pure ionic bond $\mu = e \times d = 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \times 141.4 \times 10^{-12} = 22.652 \times 10^{-30}$ C m $= 6.79$ D. Percentage ionic character $= \dfrac{0.79}{6.79} \times 100 = 11.6\ \%$.

marking_scheme.step: Ionic dipole moment e × d = 6.79 D

questions.stem_md: In a model of a polar bond in a gas-phase molecule, partial charges of +0.35e and −0.35e are separated by 108 pm. Calculate the dipole moment in debye. (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m)

marking_scheme.step: μ = q d in C m

questions.stem_md: A bent triatomic molecule AB₂ has two identical A–B bonds, each with a bond moment of 1.8 D, and the B–A–B angle is 106°. Using μ = 2 m cos(θ/2), calculate the dipole moment of the molecule in D.

A fuel chemist estimates the energy needed to break all the bonds in one mole of gaseous ethane, C₂H₆, into free atoms, using the bond enthalpies C–H 414 and C–C 347 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the estimate in kJ mol⁻¹?
questions.solution_md: Ethane has 6 C–H bonds and 1 C–C bond: $6 \times 414 + 347 = 2484 + 347 = 2831$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Carbon dioxide has a zero dipole moment.

**Reason (R):** Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. But the zero moment is explained by the linear shape, which makes the two equal C=O dipoles cancel, not by the difference in electronegativity — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Define bond length and bond enthalpy. How does each change when the bond order between two carbon atoms goes from 1 to 3?

answer.model_answer_md: Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of the bond in the gaseous state (the energy released when it forms). From C–C to C≡C the bond length decreases (154 → 120 pm) and the bond enthalpy increases (347 → 837 kJ mol⁻¹).

questions.solution_md: Definitions; length falls and enthalpy rises with bond order.

questions.stem_md: Define dipole moment. Why is the dipole moment of carbon dioxide zero while that of water is not?

answer.model_answer_md: The dipole moment is the product of the magnitude of the charge and the distance between the charges, μ = q × d, in debye (a vector quantity). CO₂ is linear, so the two C=O bond dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel. H₂O is bent (104.5°), so the two O–H bond dipoles do not cancel and give a resultant of about 1.85 D.

questions.solution_md: μ = q × d; CO₂ linear (cancels), H₂O bent (adds).

marking_scheme.step: Shapes: linear cancels, bent does not

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between ionic compounds and covalent compounds, one in physical state or melting point and one in electrical conduction.

answer.model_answer_md: Ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points, since strong electrostatic forces hold the ions in a lattice; covalent compounds are usually gases, liquids or soft low-melting solids, since only weak forces act between molecules. Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because ions are free to move; covalent compounds are generally non-conductors, because they contain no ions.

questions.solution_md: High against low melting point; conduct when molten or dissolved against non-conductors.

marking_scheme.step: Melting point or state compared with reason

questions.stem_md: The carbon–carbon bonds have lengths 154, 134 and 120 pm and enthalpies 347, 611 and 837 kJ mol⁻¹ in ethane, ethene and ethyne. Explain the trend and use the data to decide whether ethyne's triple bond is three times as strong as a single bond.

answer.model_answer_md: As more electron pairs are shared the nuclei are drawn closer, so the bond length decreases, and more energy is needed to break the bond, so the bond enthalpy increases. The triple bond (837 kJ mol⁻¹) is only about 2.4 times the single bond (347 kJ mol⁻¹), not three times, because the π bonds are weaker than the σ bond (the extra π bonds add about 264 and 226 kJ mol⁻¹, while σ alone is about 347).

questions.solution_md: Higher order, shorter and stronger; 837/347 = 2.4, so not three times.

marking_scheme.step: Ratio 2.4 and π bonds weaker than σ

questions.stem_md: The measured dipole moment of hydrogen fluoride is 1.91 D and its bond length is 91.7 pm. Calculate the dipole moment the molecule would have if it were completely ionic (H⁺F⁻), and hence the percentage ionic character of the bond. (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m)

answer.model_answer_md: Ionic $\mu = e \times d = 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \times 91.7 \times 10^{-12} = 14.690 \times 10^{-30}$ C m $= 4.40$ D. Percentage ionic character $= \dfrac{1.91}{4.40} \times 100 = 43.4\ \%$, so the bond is about 43 % ionic and 57 % covalent.

questions.solution_md: Ionic $\mu = 4.40$ D; ionic character $= 43.4\ \%$.

marking_scheme.step: Ionic μ = e d in C m

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain, using the shapes of the molecules, why carbon dioxide is non-polar but water is polar. [3]

(b) The S–H bond moment in H₂S is 0.70 D (given) and the H–S–H angle is 92°. Calculate the dipole moment of H₂S using μ = 2 m cos(θ/2). [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The C=O and O–H bonds are both polar because O is more electronegative than C or H. CO₂ is linear, O=C=O, so the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel: μ = 0, non-polar. H₂O is bent (104.5°) because of the two lone pairs on oxygen, so the two O–H dipoles add to a resultant of about 1.85 D: polar.

(b) $\mu = 2 \times 0.70 \times \cos(92°/2) = 1.40 \times \cos 46° = 1.40 \times 0.695 = 0.97$ D.

questions.solution_md: Linear cancels, bent adds; $\mu = 0.97$ D.

questions.stem_md: The ammonium ion in a lawn fertiliser has four N–H single bonds and no lone pair on nitrogen. The formal charge on the nitrogen atom is:
questions.solution_md: Formal charge = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − ½ bonding electrons = 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a study of electron-deficient compounds, which of the following molecules has a central atom with an incomplete octet?

options.text_md: CH₄, with eight electrons round carbon
BF₃, with six electrons round boron
NH₃, with eight electrons round nitrogen
H₂O, with eight electrons round oxygen

questions.solution_md: Boron has three valence electrons and forms three B–F bonds, so it has only 6 electrons round it. In CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O the central atoms have octets — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Phosphorus forms both PCl₃ and PCl₅, but nitrogen forms NCl₃ and no NCl₅. This is because, in the excited state:

options.text_md: phosphorus can promote a 3s electron into a vacant 3d orbital, but nitrogen has no 2d orbitals
nitrogen is more electronegative than chlorine
phosphorus has seven valence electrons while nitrogen has five
nitrogen atoms are too large to bond with five chlorine atoms

questions.solution_md: P (3s² 3p³) can reach 3s¹ 3p³ 3d¹ with five unpaired electrons (covalency 5). N has only the n = 2 shell with no d orbitals, so its covalency is limited to 3 (or 4 with a lone pair) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the compounds SCl₂, SF₄ and SF₆, sulfur shows the covalencies of respectively:

options.text_md: 2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 3
2, 4 and 6
2, 6 and 4

questions.solution_md: Sulfur has 2 unpaired electrons in the ground state (covalency 2), 4 after promotion of one 3p electron to 3d, and 6 after promotion of a 3s electron as well — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student draws the perchlorate ion with chlorine joined to four oxygen atoms by single bonds only, with no lone pair on chlorine. Calculate the formal charge on the chlorine atom in this structure.
questions.solution_md: Formal charge $= 7 - 0 - \tfrac12(8) = +3$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Nitrogen can form a pentafluoride, NF₅, by promoting one 2s electron to a vacant 2d orbital.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The second shell (n = 2) has no d orbitals, so nitrogen cannot expand its octet or have a covalency of 5.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion is +1.

**Reason (R):** The nitrogen atom in the ammonium ion carries a lone pair of electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1. R is false: all four pairs round nitrogen are bond pairs, so there is no lone pair — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Nitrogen forms NF₅ in the same way that phosphorus forms PF₅.

**Reason (R):** The second shell of nitrogen contains vacant 2d orbitals.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is false: NF₅ does not exist. R is false: there are no d orbitals in the n = 2 shell — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A Lewis structure of ozone is O=O–O. The central oxygen has one lone pair and three bonds, the oxygen joined by the single bond has three lone pairs, and the one joined by the double bond has two lone pairs. Calculate the formal charge on each of the three oxygen atoms.

answer.model_answer_md: Formal charge = V − L − B/2. Central O: 6 − 2 − ½(6) = +1. Oxygen with the single bond: 6 − 6 − ½(2) = -1. Oxygen with the double bond: 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 0. The sum is 0, the charge on the ozone molecule.

questions.solution_md: +1 on the central O; −1 on the single-bonded O; 0 on the double-bonded O.

questions.stem_md: Using electronic configurations, explain why phosphorus shows covalencies of 3 and 5, whereas nitrogen shows only 3.

answer.model_answer_md: Phosphorus is 3s² 3p³: three unpaired 3p electrons give covalency 3 (PCl₃). With a vacant 3d subshell, one 3s electron can be promoted to 3d, giving 3s¹ 3p³ 3d¹ with five unpaired electrons and covalency 5 (PCl₅). Nitrogen (2s² 2p³) has no 2d orbitals, so it cannot be promoted and its covalency is 3 only.

questions.solution_md: P: 3s¹ 3p³ 3d¹ gives 5; N has no d orbitals.

marking_scheme.step: P: ground state covalency 3 and promotion to 3d gives 5
N: no d orbitals in n = 2

questions.stem_md: Give one example each of a molecule with an incomplete octet and a molecule with an expanded octet. State the number of electrons round the central atom in each, and say why the second type is possible for phosphorus but not for nitrogen.

answer.model_answer_md: Incomplete octet: BF₃, in which boron has only 6 electrons (or BeCl₂, with 4). Expanded octet: PCl₅, in which phosphorus has 10 electrons (or SF₆, with 12). Phosphorus is in the third period and has vacant 3d orbitals that can hold the extra electrons after promotion; nitrogen, in the second period, has no d orbitals, so it cannot exceed an octet.

questions.solution_md: BF₃ (6) and PCl₅ (10); phosphorus has 3d orbitals, nitrogen does not.

marking_scheme.step: 3d orbitals for P, none for N

questions.stem_md: Sulfur forms SCl₂, SF₄ and SF₆. Write the outer electronic configuration of the sulfur atom in the state that gives each covalency, and name the covalency in each compound.

answer.model_answer_md: SCl₂, covalency 2: ground state 3s² 3p⁴ (two unpaired 3p electrons). SF₄, covalency 4: first excited state 3s² 3p³ 3d¹ (four unpaired electrons, one 3p electron promoted to 3d). SF₆, covalency 6: second excited state 3s¹ 3p³ 3d² (six unpaired electrons, one 3s and one 3p electron promoted).

questions.solution_md: Covalencies 2, 4, 6 from 3s² 3p⁴; 3s² 3p³ 3d¹; 3s¹ 3p³ 3d².

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the expression used to calculate the formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure. [1]

(b) In one Lewis structure of the nitrate ion, nitrogen has one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds and no lone pair. The doubly bonded oxygen has two lone pairs and each singly bonded oxygen has three lone pairs. Calculate the formal charge on nitrogen and on each kind of oxygen, and show that the charges add up to the charge on the ion. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Formal charge = (valence electrons of the free atom) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½ (bonding electrons).

(b) N: 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1. Doubly bonded O: 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 0. Each singly bonded O: 6 − 6 − ½(2) = -1. Sum: +1 + 0 + 2(−1) = -1, which is the charge on the ion, NO₃⁻.

questions.solution_md: Formal charges +1 on N, 0 and −1 on the oxygens; sum −1.

questions.stem_md: A student arranges the chlorides of the Group 1 metals LiCl, NaCl, KCl and RbCl in a chart. Which one has the most covalent character?

options.text_md: RbCl, because Rb⁺ is the largest cation
NaCl, because Na⁺ has the highest charge
all four are equally covalent as the anion is the same
LiCl, because Li⁺ is the smallest cation and polarises the chloride ion most

questions.solution_md: Among cations of equal charge, the smallest has the greatest polarising power (highest charge density), so LiCl has the most covalent character — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Anhydrous aluminium chloride sublimes easily and dissolves in organic solvents, while sodium chloride does not. By Fajan’s rules the better explanation is:

options.text_md: the Al³⁺ ion is larger than Na⁺ and so shares electrons more easily
the chloride ion in AlCl₃ is smaller than in NaCl
aluminium is less electronegative than sodium
the small, highly charged Al³⁺ ion strongly polarises the chloride ion, giving much covalent character

questions.solution_md: Al³⁺ (53.5 pm, charge 3+) has a far greater charge density than Na⁺ (102 pm, charge 1+), so it distorts the Cl⁻ cloud strongly and the bond has considerable covalent character — option (d).

questions.stem_md: For a given cation, which of the anions F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻ is the most easily polarised?

options.text_md: F⁻, because it is the most electronegative
Cl⁻, because it has the highest charge density
I⁻, because its large size means the outer electrons are held loosely
all are equally polarised as each has a single negative charge

questions.solution_md: A large anion has its outer electrons far from the nucleus and weakly held, so it is distorted most easily: I⁻ (220 pm) is the most polarisable — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? According to Fajan’s rules, a small cation of high charge polarises an anion more strongly than a large cation of low charge.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The greater the charge density of the cation, the more the anion cloud is distorted, and the greater the covalent character of the bond.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lithium iodide has more covalent character than lithium fluoride.

**Reason (R):** The iodide ion is larger and more easily polarised than the fluoride ion.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The large I⁻ ion is distorted far more readily by Li⁺ than the small F⁻ ion, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State two factors, one about the cation and one about the anion, that increase the covalent character of an ionic bond according to Fajan’s rules.

answer.model_answer_md: The covalent character increases when the cation is small and has a high charge (high polarising power), and when the anion is large and has a high charge (easily polarised), because the cation then distorts the electron cloud of the anion and some electron density is shared between the ions.

questions.solution_md: Small, highly charged cation; large, highly charged anion.

questions.stem_md: Lithium chloride dissolves in ethanol while sodium chloride does not. Using the ionic radii Li⁺ 76 pm and Na⁺ 102 pm and the charge-to-radius ratio z/r, explain which compound is the more covalent and why this leads to the observed solubility.

answer.model_answer_md: z/r for Li⁺ = 1/76 = 13.2 × 10⁻³ pm⁻¹; for Na⁺ = 1/102 = 9.8 × 10⁻³ pm⁻¹. Li⁺ is smaller, has the greater charge density (1.34 times that of Na⁺) and polarises the chloride ion more, so LiCl has more covalent character than NaCl. A compound with more covalent character is less strongly ionic, and dissolves in less polar organic solvents such as ethanol.

questions.solution_md: z/r: Li⁺ 13.2, Na⁺ 9.8 (× 10⁻³ pm⁻¹); LiCl more covalent and soluble in ethanol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Fajan's rules for the polarisation of an anion by a cation. [3]

(b) Arrange NaCl, MgCl₂ and AlCl₃ in the order of increasing covalent character, using the z/r values of Na⁺ (102 pm), Mg²⁺ (72 pm) and Al³⁺ (53.5 pm) and giving your reason. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The covalent character of an ionic bond increases with (i) a small size of the cation, (ii) a large charge on the cation, (iii) a large size of the anion, and (iv) a large charge on the anion; cations without a noble gas configuration (such as Ag⁺ and Cu⁺, with 18 outer electrons) also polarise more than noble-gas-type cations of the same size.

(b) z/r: Na⁺ = 9.8, Mg²⁺ = 27.8, Al³⁺ = 56.1 (× 10⁻³ pm⁻¹). The order of increasing covalent character is NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃, since the polarising power of the cation (charge density) increases in this order.

questions.solution_md: Fajan's rules; NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃ (z/r 9.8 < 27.8 < 56.1).

marking_scheme.step: (a) Cation: small size and large charge
(a) Anion: large size and large charge

questions.stem_md: Ammonia is the working fluid of a large cold-storage plant. By VSEPR theory its molecule has the shape and approximate H–N–H angle:

options.text_md: trigonal planar, 120°
trigonal pyramidal, about 107°
tetrahedral, 109.5°

questions.solution_md: N has 4 electron pairs (3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair), arranged tetrahedrally; the lone pair pushes the bond pairs together, so the molecule is pyramidal with an angle of about 107° — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The H–O–H angle in a water molecule, 104.5°, is smaller than the tetrahedral angle 109.5° because:

options.text_md: the two lone pairs repel the bond pairs more strongly than the bond pairs repel one another
oxygen is larger than hydrogen
the bond pairs repel one another more strongly than the lone pairs do
oxygen forms double bonds with hydrogen

questions.solution_md: Lone pairs occupy more space, so the repulsion order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, and the bond pairs are squeezed closer — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In SF₄ the sulfur atom has four bond pairs and one lone pair. The lone pair takes an equatorial position of the trigonal bipyramid, so the shape of the molecule is:

options.text_md: square planar
see-saw
tetrahedral
trigonal bipyramidal

questions.solution_md: S has 6 + 4 = 10 electrons round it (5 pairs). With the lone pair equatorial, four atoms remain: two axial and two equatorial, giving a see-saw shape — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Xenon difluoride has the shape:

options.text_md: bent, because the two lone pairs repel the bond pairs
linear, because the three lone pairs lie in the equatorial plane and the two F atoms are axial
T-shaped, because there are two lone pairs on xenon
linear, because xenon has no lone pairs

questions.solution_md: Xe has 8 + 2 = 10 electrons (5 pairs): 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs. The three lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions, leaving the two F atoms axial, 180° apart — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In VSEPR theory the repulsion between two lone pairs is weaker than the repulsion between two bond pairs.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A lone pair is attracted by only one nucleus and spreads out more, so lone pair–lone pair repulsion is the strongest of the three kinds.

questions.stem_md: The number of lone pairs on the central xenon atom in XeF₄ is ___.
questions.solution_md: Xe has 8 + 4 = 12 electrons round it (6 pairs): 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, giving a square planar molecule.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The SF₄ molecule has a see-saw shape.

**Reason (R):** Sulfur tetrafluoride is a gas at room temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true (SF₄ boils at about −38 °C). But the physical state says nothing about shape: the see-saw shape follows from the five electron pairs round S (four bond pairs, one lone pair, the lone pair in an equatorial position) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The H–N–H angle in ammonia is 107°, while the H–C–H angle in methane is 109.5° and the H–O–H angle in water is 104.5°. Explain the three values using VSEPR theory.

answer.model_answer_md: All three central atoms have four electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally. CH₄ has four bond pairs, all equal, so the angle is the ideal 109.5°. NH₃ has one lone pair, which repels the bond pairs more strongly, so the angle falls to 107°. H₂O has two lone pairs, so the repulsion on the bond pairs is greater still and the angle is 104.5°.

questions.solution_md: Zero, one and two lone pairs: 109.5°, 107°, 104.5°.

marking_scheme.step: Four electron pairs in each; CH₄ ideal
Lone pairs compress the angle: 107° and 104.5°

questions.stem_md: Using VSEPR theory, predict the shapes of SF₄ and XeF₂. For each, give the number of bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom and the positions of the lone pairs.

answer.model_answer_md: SF₄: S has 6 + 4 = 10 electrons, so 5 pairs: 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair. The lone pair is equatorial (to reduce repulsion), so the shape is see-saw. XeF₂: Xe has 8 + 2 = 10 electrons, 5 pairs: 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs. The three lone pairs are equatorial, so the two F atoms are axial and the molecule is linear (180°).

questions.solution_md: SF₄ see-saw (4 bp, 1 lp); XeF₂ linear (2 bp, 3 lp, all equatorial).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Predict the shapes of SF₆, ClF₃ and BrF₅ using VSEPR theory, giving the numbers of bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom of each. [3]

(b) State the hybridisation of the central atom in each of the three molecules. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) SF₆: 6 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs, octahedral (90°). ClF₃: Cl has 7 + 3 = 10 electrons, 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, both lone pairs equatorial, so T-shaped. BrF₅: Br has 7 + 5 = 12 electrons, 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, square pyramidal.

(b) SF₆: sp³d² (six pairs). ClF₃: sp³d (five pairs, trigonal bipyramidal arrangement). BrF₅: sp³d² (six pairs, octahedral arrangement).

questions.solution_md: SF₆ octahedral; ClF₃ T-shaped; BrF₅ square pyramidal; sp³d², sp³d, sp³d².

questions.stem_md: Each carbon atom in ethene, the monomer of polythene, has three sigma bonds and one pi bond. Its hybridisation is:

options.text_md: sp³, with tetrahedral bonds at 109.5°
sp, with linear bonds at 180°
sp³d, with trigonal bipyramidal bonds
sp², with trigonal planar bonds at about 120°

questions.solution_md: Three σ bonds use three sp² hybrid orbitals (120° apart, in a plane); the remaining unhybridised p orbital forms the π bond — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Phosphorus pentachloride, used in a chlorination reaction, has five P–Cl sigma bonds. The hybridisation of phosphorus and the shape of the molecule are:

options.text_md: sp³d², octahedral
sp³, tetrahedral
sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal
sp², trigonal planar

questions.solution_md: One 3s, three 3p and one 3d orbital mix to give five sp³d orbitals directed to the corners of a trigonal bipyramid — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The nitrogen atom in ammonia is sp³ hybridised, yet the molecule is not tetrahedral. The reason is that:

options.text_md: the nitrogen atom uses three p orbitals and no s orbital
two of the sp³ orbitals hold lone pairs
one of the four sp³ orbitals holds a lone pair, so only three bonds point to atoms and the shape is pyramidal
ammonia is sp² hybridised in its excited state

questions.solution_md: Four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron; one holds the lone pair and three form N–H bonds, giving a trigonal pyramidal molecule — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In sulfur hexafluoride the six S–F bonds are all equal and directed along the three axes of an octahedron. The hybridisation of sulfur is:

options.text_md: sp³d²
sp³d
sp³
sp²d

questions.solution_md: One 3s, three 3p and two 3d orbitals mix to form six equivalent sp³d² orbitals pointing to the corners of an octahedron — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each molecule with the hybridisation of its central atom.

options.text_md: BeCl₂
BF₃
CH₄
PCl₅

questions.solution_md: BeCl₂ → s (sp); BF₃ → p (sp²); CH₄ → r (sp³); PCl₅ → q (sp³d).

questions.stem_md: What is hybridisation? State two features of hybrid orbitals.

answer.model_answer_md: Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies in the same atom to form the same number of new, equivalent orbitals, called hybrid orbitals. The hybrid orbitals have the same energy and shape, and are directed in space at fixed angles that give the geometry of the molecule (for example four sp³ orbitals at 109.5°). Their number equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed.

questions.solution_md: Mixing of orbitals into equivalent orbitals; same energy and shape, fixed directions.

questions.stem_md: Boron trifluoride is planar while ammonia is pyramidal. State the hybridisation of the central atom in each and explain how it accounts for the shape.

answer.model_answer_md: In BF₃ boron promotes a 2s electron to 2p (2s¹ 2p²) and the one s and two p orbitals give three sp² orbitals at 120° in a plane; each forms a σ bond with a fluorine atom, so BF₃ is trigonal planar. In NH₃ nitrogen uses one 2s and three 2p orbitals to give four sp³ orbitals directed to the corners of a tetrahedron: three form N–H σ bonds and the fourth holds the lone pair, so the molecule is trigonal pyramidal (H–N–H about 107°).

questions.solution_md: BF₃ sp², planar; NH₃ sp³ with one lone pair, pyramidal.

marking_scheme.step: NH₃: sp³ with a lone pair
Shape linked to the orbitals used for bonding

questions.stem_md: Describe the bonding in ethene in terms of hybridisation: name the hybridisation of each carbon, the orbitals that overlap to form the C–C and C–H bonds, and the number of sigma and pi bonds in the molecule.

answer.model_answer_md: Each carbon is sp² hybridised: three sp² orbitals in a plane at 120° and one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the plane. Two sp² orbitals of each carbon overlap with the 1s orbitals of hydrogen to form four C–H σ bonds; the remaining sp² orbitals overlap head-on to form the C–C σ bond. The two parallel 2p orbitals overlap sideways to form the C–C π bond. In all there are 5 σ bonds and 1 π bond.

questions.solution_md: sp² carbons; C–H σ (sp²–s), C–C σ (sp²–sp²) and π (p–p); 5 σ and 1 π.

marking_scheme.step: σ bonds from sp² overlap (C–H and C–C)
π bond from sideways p overlap; 5 σ and 1 π
